extra.message: Cleartext transmission of sensitive information — Flask app runs without SSL/TLS

metadata.proof: SOURCE: The Flask application is started at run.py line 10 with app.run(debug=debug_mode) - no ssl_context argument, meaning the development server binds only to HTTP (no HTTPS). The login form at routes.py sends username and password via POST over this unencrypted channel. The session cookie is transmitted in cleartext on every request. SINK: Any network intermediary (compromised router, ARP-spoofed WiFi, ISP) can intercept credentials and session tokens passively.

extra.message: Unrestricted file upload in profile picture endpoint — no content-type validation

metadata.proof: SOURCE: The file object comes from request.files['profile_picture'] at line 200, which is fully attacker-controlled via the multipart form submission to /update_profile. SINK: At line 214, file.save() writes the raw bytes to disk without any content-type validation, magic-byte verification, or file signature check. extra.message: No CSRF protection on any state-changing endpoint

metadata.proof: The application never imports or enables Flask-WTF CSRF protection, nor does it include any custom CSRF token validation. Every POST endpoint — login (line 21), signup (line 65), update_profile (line 168), upload_file (line 248), delete_file (line 340) — accepts requests without requiring a CSRF token. An attacker can craft an HTML form that auto-submits to /update_profile and change the victim's email, country, role, or permissions if the victim visits a malicious page while logged in.

extra.message: Session cookie missing Secure flag

metadata.proof: run.py configures SESSION_COOKIE_NAME and SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY but never sets SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE; Flask defaults this to False. The session cookie is transmitted over unencrypted HTTP, allowing network attackers to capture the session token via passive eavesdropping (session hijacking). Even if HTTPS were added later, this cookie would still be sent over HTTP.

extra.message: Session cookie missing SameSite attribute

metadata.proof: run.py never sets SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE; Flask defaults to None, producing no SameSite attribute on the Set-Cookie header. This makes cross-site request forgery substantially easier because the cookie is sent on all cross-origin requests, including simple POST forms from an attacker's page.

extra.message: Session object printed to server logs exposing session data

metadata.proof: In UserProfileUpdate.post() at api_v1.py line 182, the entire Flask session dictionary is written to stdout via print(session) on every request. The session object contains the username and user_id of the currently logged-in user. In containerised or shared-server deployments where logs are aggregated (e.g., Docker, ELK, CloudWatch), any team member with log access can see every user's session data, enabling session hijacking and user enumeration.

extra.message: No rate limiting or brute-force protection on login or signup

extra.message: Unbounded file listing on /dashboard enables memory-exhaustion denial of service

metadata.proof: SOURCE: The /dashboard handler (line 129) runs a SELECT query on the files table filtered by user_id with no LIMIT/OFFSET clause. SINK: Line 141 materializes every row into a Python list via fetchall() in a single allocation. Combined with the unrestricted file upload at routes.py:247-264 (no MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH, no per-user upload cap, no rate limiting), an attacker can script mass uploads to inflate their file count, then request GET /dashboard to cause fetchall() to buffer all filenames — each a Python string object — into memory until OOM kills the process. No pagination, no server-side LIMIT, and no cursor iteration using fetchone() bounds the per-request memory consumption.
